study.title: Genome-integrated engineering of <i>Escherichia coli</i> Nissle 1917 enables sustained gut-local biosynthesis of 5-hydroxytryptophan

cover.headline: Engineered gut bacteria were modified to **produce the serotonin precursor 5-HTP** inside the intestine.

slides.title: If this approach holds up, it could allow serotonin precursors to be made locally without oral pills.
slides.body:
Delivering neuroactive compounds locally in the intestine might sidestep some of the absorption and stability issues that come with supplements. But engineering microbes to produce these molecules consistently has been hard, especially when the genetic circuits are unstable and get lost over time.

A genome-integrated probiotic system could offer sustained, gut-local biosynthesis without needing antibiotics or inducers to keep the pathway active. That matters if the goal is eventual therapeutic use in living organisms.

slides.title: Researchers integrated a 5-HTP biosynthesis pathway into the genome of E. coli Nissle 1917, a clinically used probiotic.
slides.body:
The team chose Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 because it already has an established safety profile for intestinal use. They inserted the entire pathway directly into the bacterial chromosome to avoid plasmid loss, and they used constitutive expression to eliminate the need for chemical inducers.

They also added modules to produce and regenerate BH4, a cofactor the bacteria need but that is scarce in the gut environment. The engineered strain was then tested in lab culture, after gut passage in mice, and in a reserpine-induced depression model.

slides.title: The engineered strain produced 5-HTP at 863.2 mg/L and stayed stable without antibiotics or selection pressure.
slides.body:
The genome-integrated version maintained 5-HTP production in the lab even under non-selective conditions, and retained its biosynthetic capacity after passing through the mouse intestine. Plasmid-based versions lost production rapidly under the same conditions.

In mice, a single dose caused a transient spike in plasma 5-HTP. Repeated dosing led to fluctuations in gut bacterial numbers and local biosynthesis. Treatment with the engineered probiotic improved behavioral phenotypes and modulated brain metabolites linked to serotonin in the reserpine model.

caveats: This was done in cells in a dish and mice, not humans. Most findings in cells and mice do not carry over to people.
The behavioral effects were measured in a pharmacologically induced mouse model, not in animals with naturally occurring mood disorders.

caption: Engineering gut bacteria to make serotonin precursors locally could bypass some of the instability that plagues oral supplements. This team inserted the entire 5-HTP biosynthesis pathway into the genome of E. coli Nissle 1917, a clinically used probiotic, and added machinery to produce the cofactor BH4 on-site. The result was stable production at 863.2 mg/L in the lab and sustained activity after gut passage in mice. In a reserpine depression model, the engineered probiotic improved behavior and shifted brain serotonin metabolites. Published in Synthetic and Systems Biotechnology, the experiments used bacterial cultures and mouse models. The work has not been tested in humans. Full study: doi.org/10.1016/j.synbio.2026.08.002 — Send this to anyone who keeps arguing that chromosomal integration doesn't solve the plasmid stability problem.

source.abstract: 5-Hydroxytryptophan (5-HTP) is a functional precursor of serotonin; however, achieving sustained 5-HTP production in vivo by engineered microbes remains challenging. To address this, we developed a genome-integrated engineered probiotic system enabling gut-local biosynthesis of 5-HTP. Escherichia coli Nissle 1917 (EcN), a clinically validated probiotic with an established safety profile for intestinal application, was selected as the chassis. Constitutive expression was employed to eliminate inducer dependence, while genomic integration was used to enhance genetic stability and avoid reliance on antibiotic selection for pathway maintenance. In addition, BH4 biosynthesis and regeneration modules were incorporated to address the limited endogenous BH4 availability in the gut environment. Different administration strategies were systematically evaluated to characterize in vivo performance. Notably, our results showed that the hTPH2 hydroxylation module, together with the BH4 biosynthesis and regeneration system, supported 5-HTP biosynthesis in EcN. The engineered EcN strain achieved a 5-HTP titer of 863.2 mg/L, the highest level reported in EcN-based systems. Under non-selective conditions, EcN Pconst-5-HTP carrying the chromosomally integrated pathway maintained stable 5-HTP production in vitro and retained 5-HTP-producing capacity after intestinal passage, whereas plasmid loss in non-integrated constructs resulted in a pronounced decrease in production. In vivo analysis showed that single-dose administration induced a transient elevation in plasma 5-HTP, whereas repeated dosing generated reproducible, time-dependent fluctuations in fecal bacterial abundance and gut-local biosynthetic activity. Treatment with the engineered probiotic further improved behavioral phenotypes and modulated brain 5-HT-related metabolites in a reserpine-induced mouse model. Together, these findings provide a translational framework linking in vitro 5-HTP production by engineered probiotics to their in vivo functional performance.
